title: Migration 71 — the seventeen tables that told the auditor “nothing here”
description: Builds the world production was in on 2026-08-12 for the SEVENTEEN tables that never errored and never showed the auditing role anything: the base schema, then 9, 10, 17, 30, 34, 36, 39, 40, 41, 42, 43, 44 and 67, then a pre-apply stage that creates both auditing roles AND grants them SELECT on all seventeen — because the grants are the whole trap. On production `has_table_privilege` was already true for both roles on all seventeen and every read still returned 0: the policies are scoped TO authenticated and neither role is a member, so no permissive policy applied and PostgreSQL returned nothing. Not an error. Nothing. Two were provably lying: public_intake_attempts held 14 rows and read as 0; security_settings held 1 and read as 0. Unlike migration 70 this is purely additive — none of the seventeen carries a RESTRICTIVE policy and none carries a policy scoped TO public, so there is no plan-time EXECUTE trap and no existing policy is touched. VERIFY B is the section that matters: on these tables the DEFECT IS A ZERO, so counting rows or checking for no-error would pass identically before and after. B writes one row into each of the seventeen and requires each auditing role to find that specific row. C pins what an ordinary logged-in non-admin sees across all seventeen — values measured by running the same probe with 71 applied and with 71 rolled back and confirming the two were identical — and asserts in both directions, including that the two deliberately-open tables still read 1. Rollback drops seventeen policies and nothing else, which is why it is so much shorter than 70's.

verify.note: A structural: seventeen auditor policies on PUBLIC naming both roles, and nothing else newly on PUBLIC — a policy there would be planned for the auditing roles and reintroduce migration 70's plan-time EXECUTE trap. B behavioural and the whole point: a row that IS there must be VISIBLE to each auditing role in each of the seventeen. Asserting visibility rather than absence-of-error is not stylistic here — the defect being fixed IS a silent zero, so a no-error check passes on a broken database and a count-is-zero check passes on an empty one. C behavioural, both directions: an ordinary non-admin gains nothing, is still refused public_intake_attempts at the privilege layer, and still reads the two tables whose own migrations grant USING(true) — the last of these catches 71 breaking the app rather than widening it. D the auditing role still cannot write. E the apply recorded itself. F neither auditing role owns a SECURITY DEFINER function, the standing condition that makes the current_user comparison safe and whose reach 71 widens. That this VERIFY fails once 71 is rolled back is not asserted by any fixture key — the harness has none, and inventing one would be a claim nothing checks; it is proven by re-running the VERIFY on a rolled-back cluster.
